A representation is an internal description used by a model or a later task.
To interpret a representation-learning claim, identify what is optimised, what is frozen, and what information the representation can access.
CLIP and SigLIP provide concrete examples of learning encoders from paired images and text.

## Learning representations and adapting to tasks {#representations}

Representation learning produces features useful for some objective or later use.
Task-specific learning optimises performance on a particular prediction or control problem.
Both can occur in the same end-to-end model.
Task learning is not a synonym for in-context learning or zero-shot generalisation.

| Evaluation or adaptation | What is updated or supplied? |
|---|---|
| Linear probe | Freeze the feature extractor and fit a linear prediction head. |
| Fine-tuning | Update some or all pretrained parameters for the target task. |
| Zero-shot evaluation | Evaluate the stated task without task-specific training examples or parameter updates, under the paper's protocol. |
| In-context learning | Provide examples or instructions in the input context, ordinarily without updating model parameters. |

An end-to-end training objective connects inputs to task outputs through a shared optimisation process.
A modular system splits responsibilities into components; some modular systems are still trained jointly.
Late fusion processes modalities separately before combining representations or scores.
These properties should be established from the actual computation and gradient paths.
[CLIP](../../literature-review/multimodal/clip.qmd), [DINO](../../literature-review/vision/dino.qmd), and [PaliGemma](../../literature-review/multimodal/paligemma.qmd) illustrate different representation and adaptation choices.

## Context and position in sequence representations {#sequence-terms}

Self-attention uses query and source representations from the same sequence; its mask determines which positions can communicate.
Cross-attention reads a different source sequence.
Causal attention prevents access to later positions, while bidirectional attention permits both directions among allowed tokens.
Neither definition alone says how training examples were collected.

Absolute positional representations can be learned or fixed; they are not always fixed vectors.
Relative position methods encode position differences or transform queries and keys so their scores depend on relative positions.
A token's contextual representation incorporates information from the positions its model permits it to read.
Diffusion time embeddings identify a noise level or generative step, distinct from the position of a word or robot command.
See [attention](attention.qmd#projections), [representations](representations.qmd), and [generative time](generative-sampling.qmd#objects).

## CLIP and SigLIP: what the visual encoder learned {#clip-and-siglip}

Both methods train image and text encoders using paired examples.
For a batch of $B$ pairs, let $u_i$ and $v_j$ be unit-normalised image and text embeddings.
The dot product $u_i^\top v_j$ measures their cosine similarity.
The original pairing provides positive labels when $i=j$; other pairings provide negatives, even though some can also be semantically compatible.

CLIP uses scores $s_{ij}=t\,u_i^\top v_j$, with learned positive scale $t$.
For image $i$, its matching caption competes with the batch's other captions:

$$
  p(j\mid i)=\frac{e^{s_{ij}}}{\sum_{m=1}^{B}e^{s_{im}}}.
$$

CLIP averages image-to-text and text-to-image cross-entropies.
The latter applies the corresponding softmax down columns of the score matrix.
See [CLIP, §2.3 and Figure 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020).

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  L_{\mathrm{CLIP}}=-\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}
  \bigl[&\log p(T_i\mid I_i)\\
  &+\log p(I_i\mid T_i)\bigr].
  \end{aligned}
$$

Here $I_i$ and $T_i$ denote the paired image and caption, respectively.

SigLIP scores pairs with $s_{ij}=t\,u_i^\top v_j+b$, including learned bias $b$.
With labels $y_{ij}=1$ for matched pairs and $-1$ otherwise, its objective is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \sigma(s)&=\frac{1}{1+e^{-s}},\\
  L_{\mathrm{SigLIP}}
  &=-\frac1B\sum_{i,j=1}^{B}
  \log\sigma(y_{ij}s_{ij}).
  \end{aligned}
$$

This follows [SigLIP, Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343), including its division by $B$ rather than $B^2$.
Each pair contributes a binary logistic loss without a denominator involving other pairs.
SigLIP still uses negatives and shared encoder parameters; pairwise loss terms do not imply statistically independent embeddings or training without batches.
The pairwise decomposition permits computing and accumulating smaller blocks of pair scores.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Calculation: competition versus pairwise classification"}

Suppose one image has two caption scores, $2$ and $0$, with the first caption designated positive.
Its CLIP image-to-text probability is

$$
  p(1\mid i)=\frac{e^2}{e^2+e^0}\approx0.881.
$$

Adding a third caption with score $2$ changes this to approximately $0.468$, although the first pair's score stayed fixed.
The alternatives change the softmax denominator.

For the same numerical logits, SigLIP assigns $\sigma(2)\approx0.881$ to the first pair and $\sigma(0)=0.5$ to the second.
An additional negative pair contributes another loss term without changing either existing pair's sigmoid value.
Their values need not sum to one.
The [binary and categorical cross-entropy note](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) derives both loss forms.

:::

## Representation pretraining and policy training {#representation-pretraining-and-policy-training}

Using a SigLIP-initialised encoder does not mean a robot policy trains with SigLIP's image-text matching loss.
The pretraining objective explains how the initial visual representation was learned; downstream objectives supervise what the assembled policy must predict.
In the [$\pi_{0.5}$ paper, §IV-B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054), discrete action tokens and continuous flow outputs receive different objectives.

[FAST](../../literature-review/action/fast.qmd) explains how an action trajectory becomes discrete targets for autoregressive cross-entropy.
[Generative action models](generative-models.qmd#questions) explains noisy continuous inputs and velocity targets.
The [$\pi_{0.5}$](../../literature-review/action/pi05.qmd) and [knowledge insulation](../../literature-review/action/knowledge-insulation.qmd) notes connect these representations to the branches that receive their gradients.
